business_model.basis: Stated in Item 4 and Item 5 of the 2025 Form 20-F and the October 2026 Form 6-K.
business_model.claim: Volaris operates as an ultra-low-cost carrier providing point-to-point passenger, cargo, and mail air transportation across Mexico, the United States, Central America, and South America, targeting visiting-friends-and-relatives, cost-conscious business, and leisure travelers.
quotes: We are a ULCC incorporated under the laws of Mexico.
Our main competitive advantages are our low base fares and our focus on VFR travelers, leisure travelers and cost-conscious business travelers.
Volaris targets passengers who are visiting friends and relatives, cost-conscious business and leisure travelers in Mexico, the United States, Central, and South America.

business_model.basis: Stated in the 2025 Form 20-F statements of operations and Item 5.
business_model.claim: The company unbundles air travel by charging low base fares alongside separate fees for other passenger services—such as excess baggage, call center or third-party bookings, advance seat selection, itinerary changes, priority services, charters, and v.club memberships—generating $ 1,301,750 in fare revenues and 1,580,665 in other passenger revenues (table in USD thousands) in 2025, or 43% and 52% of total operating revenues of 3,037,516 (table in USD thousands).
quotes: This unbundling strategy has allowed us to significantly grow our non-passenger revenue and total revenue.

Other passenger services include but are not limited to fees charged for excess baggage, bookings through the call center or third-party agencies, advanced seat selection, itinerary changes, priority services (premium plus) and charters.
43% of our total operating revenues were derived from passenger fares in 2025.
52% of our total operating revenues were derived from other passenger revenues in 2025.
Total operating revenues | 3,037,516 | 3,141,876 | 3,258,973

business_model.basis: Stated in the 2025 Form 20-F and 3Q 2026 Form 6-K.
business_model.claim: Non-passenger sources—comprising other non-passenger services such as third-party sales commissions (134,483, table in USD thousands) and cargo (20,618, table in USD thousands)—accounted for U.S.$155.1 million, or 5%, of total operating revenues in 2025, alongside a loyalty program launched in 2025 and codeshare alliances with Frontier, Copa, Iberia, Hainan, and Turkish.
quotes: In 2025, we derived U.S.$155.1 million, or 5%, of our total operating revenues from these sources.
Revenues from other non-passenger services mainly include, but are not limited to, commissions charged to third parties for the sale of services.
Through these alliances, Iberia, Hainan, COPA and Turkish customers gain access to additional destinations operated by the Company.
On July 16, 2025, the Company launched its loyalty program “altitude”

business_model.basis: Stated in Item 3.D of the 2025 Form 20-F.
business_model.claim: Mexican domestic operations generated 59% of total revenues in 2025, while operations in the United States and Central and South America generated 41%.
quotes: For the year ended December 31, 2025, 59% of our total revenues were attributable to our Mexican domestic operations.
For the year ended December 31, 2025, 41% of our total revenues were attributable to our operations within these regions.

business_model.basis: Stated in Note v) Operating segments of the 3Q 2026 Form 6-K.
business_model.claim: Volaris reports only one operating segment because management monitors the company as a single business unit providing air transportation and related services.
quotes: Management of Controladora monitors the Company as a single business unit that provides air transportation and related services, accordingly it has only one operating segment.

business_model.basis: Stated in Item 4 and Item 5 of the 2025 Form 20-F.
business_model.claim: Passenger revenue is driven by capacity, load factor (84.3% in 2025), and average passenger revenue per booked passenger, using low base fares (averaging U.S. $42.0 in 2025 and discounted to as low as U.S. $0.05 or MXN $1) to shift long-distance bus passengers to air travel and expand ancillary purchases.
quotes: Passenger revenues are based upon our capacity, load factor and the average passenger revenue per booked passenger.
During 2025, our average base fare was U.S. $42.0, and we regularly offered promotional fares as low as U.S. $0.05 (MXN $1), excluding airport fees.

We set certain of our promotional fares at prices lower than bus fares for similar routes in order to stimulate demand for air travel among passengers who in the past have traveled long distances primarily by bus.

business_model.basis: Stated in Item 5 and the statement of financial position of the 2025 Form 20-F.
business_model.claim: All tickets are non-refundable and advance ticket sales are recorded as unearned transportation revenue (360,796 at year-end 2025, table in USD thousands) until recognized as revenue upon flight delivery or ticket expiration.
quotes: Ticket sales for future flights are initially recognized as contract liabilities under the caption “unearned transportation revenue” and, once we provide the transportation service or when the non-refundable ticket expires at the date of the scheduled travel, the earned revenue is recognized as passenger ticket revenues and the unearned transportation revenue is reduced by the same amount.
All of our tickets are non-refundable; however, certain tickets may be changed upon payment of a fee.

business_model.basis: Stated in Item 3.D and Item 5 of the 2025 Form 20-F.
business_model.claim: Revenue is shaped by seasonal peaks in summer, December, and Easter, macroeconomic and U.S.–Mexico immigration and tariff uncertainty, Mexico City airport slot caps (raised to 44 flights per hour in May 2025), and competition from Aeroenlaces Nacionales, Grupo Aeroméxico, U.S. carriers, New Mexicana de Aviación, and long-distance buses.
quotes: We generally expect demand to be greater during the summer, during December and around Easter, which can fall either in the first or second quarter, compared to the rest of the year.

Implementation of immigration and trade policies can adversely affect United States—Mexico travel behavior, especially in the VFR and leisure markets and could have a negative impact on our results of operations.
In May 2025, the AFAC authorized a limited increase in the maximum number of operations at the Mexico City International Airport from 43 to 44 flights per hour.
The New Mexicana de Aviación was created on June 15, 2023, as a state-owned company and started operations on December 26, 2023, further increasing our competition.

business_model.basis: Stated in the October 2026 traffic report Form 6-K.
business_model.claim: In October 2026, capacity expansion shifted toward international routes, with international ASMs rising 27.5% year-over-year to represent 50% of monthly capacity across new Guadalajara–U.S. routes while domestic RPMs declined 8.4% and consolidated load factor fell 3.5 percentage points to 82.4%.
quotes: In October, Volaris’ ASM capacity increased 7.7% year-over-year, with international ASMs growing 27.5%, reflecting the continued strategic expansion of its U.S.–Mexico transborder network.
Consolidated load factor decreased 3.5 percentage points year-over-year to 82.4%, temporarily impacted by the ramping up of the new international capacity.

business_model.basis: Stated in Item 4 of the 2025 Form 20-F.
business_model.claim: Volaris maintains a low unit cost base—reporting a 2025 CASM of U.S. 8.04 cents—through a uniform Airbus fleet (155 aircraft at year-end 2025), high asset utilization, direct sales and distribution, and variable performance-based compensation.
quotes: In 2025, our CASM was U.S. 8.04 cents, compared to an average non-stage-length adjusted CASM of U.S. 11.12 cents for the other Latin American publicly traded airlines, including Aeroméxico, Copa, and LATAM.
We have achieved this through our efficient and uniform fleet, high asset utilization, our emphasis on direct sales and distribution and our variable, performance-based compensation structure.

business_model.basis: Stated in the 2025 Form 20-F and 3Q 2026 Form 6-K.
business_model.claim: Fuel is the largest operating cost at 885,520 in 2025 (table in USD thousands), or 31% of total operating costs, leaving operating results exposed to jet fuel index fluctuations and Middle East conflict supply shocks with no fuel derivatives held as of the 2026 third-quarter report.
quotes: Fuel is a major cost component for airlines and is our largest operating expense.
The cost of fuel accounted for 38%, 33%, and 31%, of our total operating costs in 2023, 2024, and 2025, respectively.
The recent spike in the price of aircraft fuel resulting from the conflicts in Iran and the Middle East is expected to have an immediate and substantial negative impact on our results of operations.
As of the date of this report, Volaris does not have Jet Fuel derivative financial instruments.

business_model.basis: Stated in the 2025 Form 20-F statements of operations and Item 5, and the 3Q 2026 Form 6-K.
business_model.claim: Major non-fuel operating expenses in 2025 (table in USD thousands) were landing, take-off and navigation fees (544,298), salaries and benefits (451,096), right-of-use asset depreciation (448,570), owned asset and major maintenance amortization (208,176), and aircraft and engine variable lease expenses (196,082), partially offset by (222,256) in other operating income from sale-and-leaseback gains and Pratt & Whitney GTF engine inspection compensation.
quotes: Other operating income includes gains from sale and leaseback transactions and the compensation received from the manufacturer related to preventive accelerated inspections for the GTF engines.
CASM ex fuel stood at 6.23 cents, up 13.7% year-over-year, but below guidance, supported by improved fixed-cost absorption from higher-than-planned capacity and continued cost efficiencies.

The fourth quarter and full year 2026 outlook presented above includes the compensation that Volaris expects to receive for the projected grounded aircraft resulting from the GTF engine inspections, in accordance with the Company’s agreement with Pratt & Whitney.

business_model.basis: Stated in the 2025 Form 20-F and 3Q 2026 Form 6-K.
business_model.claim: Significant lease liabilities (409,125 current and 2,744,256 non-current at year-end 2025, table in USD thousands) and financial debt (261,721 current and 441,117 non-current) generated (314,139) of finance cost in 2025, while a U.S. $0.3 billion net monetary liability position in Mexican pesos and other currencies creates FX sensitivity with no FX derivatives held as of the 2026 third-quarter report.
quotes: As of December 31, 2023, 2024, and 2025, our net monetary Mexican peso and other currencies liability position denominated in U.S. dollars was U.S. $0.2 billion, U.S. $0.4 billion, and U.S. $0.3 billion, respectively.
As of the date of presentation of this report, Volaris does not have foreign exchange derivative financial instruments.
As of the date of this report, the Company holds interest rate CAPs with TIIE 28 as underlying for the Asset Backed Trust Notes.

competitive_position.basis: stated in P5 (About Volaris section of the October 2026 traffic 6-K)
competitive_position.claim: Volaris is an ultra-low-cost carrier with point-to-point operations across Mexico, the United States, Central America, and South America, operating 155 aircraft and more than 247 routes.
quotes: Since the beginning of operations in March 2006, Volaris has increased its routes from 5 to more than 247 and its fleet from 4 to 155 aircraft.
Volaris offers around 500 daily flight segments on routes that connect 46 cities in Mexico and 34 cities in the United States, Central, and South America, with one of the youngest fleets in Mexico.

competitive_position.basis: stated in P1 (Item 4 Overview) and P3 (Item 5 Competition and CASM table)
competitive_position.claim: Volaris had the lowest CASM among Latin American publicly traded airlines in 2025 at U.S. 8.04 cents, compared with averages of U.S. 11.12 cents for other Latin American peers and U.S. 16.77 cents for U.S.-based target market competitors.
quotes: These low base fares are facilitated by our low CASM, which is the lowest among Latin American publicly traded airlines.

In 2025, our CASM was U.S. 8.04 cents, compared to an average non-stage length adjusted CASM of U.S. 11.12 cents for the other Latin American publicly traded airlines, including Aeroméxico, Copa, and LATAM.
We have achieved this through our efficient and uniform fleet, high asset utilization, our emphasis on direct sales and distribution and our variable, performance-based compensation structure.

competitive_position.basis: stated in P4 (Q3 2026 6-K narrative and Fourth Quarter 2026 Guidance table)
competitive_position.claim: Volaris experienced year-over-year unit cost inflation excluding fuel in 2026, with third-quarter CASM ex fuel rising 13.7% to 6.23 cents and fourth-quarter guidance at ~6.50 cents.
quotes: CASM ex fuel stood at 6.23 cents, up 13.7% year-over-year, but below guidance, supported by improved fixed-cost absorption from higher-than-planned capacity and continued cost efficiencies.

Volaris had 34.0% of the domestic market, according to the AFAC.
We have substantial market presence in the top airports in Mexico (based on number of passengers): Cancun, Guadalajara, Mexico City, and Tijuana.

competitive_position.claim: In 2025, Volaris held an 11.8% international market share to and from Mexico, a 44.9% share on the Mexico–U.S. routes it operates, and a 15.6% share across all Mexico–U.S. routes.
quotes: As of 2025, our international market share considering all airlines flying internationally to and from Mexico, increased 0.4pp to 11.8%, compared to our market share in December 2024.
We reached 44.9% market share on the routes that we operate and 15.6% market share considering all routes between Mexico and the United States in 2025, according to the AFAC.

competitive_position.claim: Volaris achieved an 84.3% average load factor and an 80.2% on-time performance rate in 2025, between the 85.2 % Latin American peer average and the 82.1% U.S. target-market peer average.
quotes: In 2025, our average load factor was 84.3%, compared to an average load factor of 85.2 % for the other Latin American publicly traded airlines and 82.1% for our U.S.-based publicly traded target market competitors.
We strive to deliver on-time performance to our customers, with an 80.2% on-time performance rate in 2025.

competitive_position.claim: In October 2026, international capacity reached 50% of total capacity as international ASMs grew 27.5% year-over-year and Volaris added new Guadalajara–U.S. routes, while consolidated load factor decreased 3.5 percentage points to 82.4%.
quotes: In October, Volaris’ ASM capacity increased 7.7% year-over-year, with international ASMs growing 27.5%, reflecting the continued strategic expansion of its U.S.–Mexico transborder network.
In October, Volaris started operating five new routes connecting Guadalajara to Atlanta, Boston, Nashville, Raleigh-Durham, and Washington D.C.
Consolidated load factor decreased 3.5 percentage points year-over-year to 82.4%, temporarily impacted by the ramping up of the new international capacity.

competitive_position.basis: stated in P1 (Item 4 Overview) and P4 (Q3 2026 6-K footnotes and revenue recognition)
competitive_position.claim: Volaris expanded network connectivity through codeshare alliances with Frontier Airlines, Copa Airlines, Iberia, Hainan Airlines, and Turkish, and launched its altitude loyalty program in 2025.
quotes: In 2025, we entered into additional codeshare agreements with Copa Airlines, Iberia and Hainan Airlines as part of our efforts to expand our network connectivity, complementing our existing arrangement with Frontier Airlines.
Through these alliances, Iberia, Hainan, COPA and Turkish customers gain access to additional destinations operated by the Company.
On July 16, 2025, the Company launched its loyalty program “altitude”

competitive_position.basis: stated in P1 (Item 4 Concession and Permits)
competitive_position.claim: Volaris holds a Mexican federal government Concession extended for a 20-year term starting in 2020, authorizing domestic regular passenger, cargo, and mail air transportation.
quotes: Through our subsidiary Volaris Opco, we hold (i) the Concession, which authorizes us to provide domestic regular passenger, cargo and mail air transportation services within Mexico, (ii) a permit for domestic charter air transportation passenger services, and (iii) a permit for international regular passenger and charter passenger air transportation services.
On February 24, 2020, our Concession was extended for a 20-year term starting on May 9, 2020.

competitive_position.basis: stated in P1 and P3 (Proposed Transaction with Viva)
competitive_position.claim: Volaris and Viva signed a Business Combination Agreement in 2025 to merge Viva into Volaris, with shareholders approving the deal in 2026 and pre-merger Volaris and Viva shareholders expected to hold approximately 50% and 48% of the combined company, respectively, pending regulatory approvals.
quotes: On December 18, 2025, the Company and Viva entered into the Business Combination Agreement, pursuant to which, subject to the terms and conditions of the Business Combination Agreement, Viva will be merged with and into Volaris with Volaris continuing thereafter as the surviving entity.

The completion of the Merger is subject to certain closing conditions, including required regulatory approvals (including under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976, Mexican competition authorities, Colombian aviation authorities, and the Mexican foreign investment commission).

competitive_position.basis: stated in P2 (Item 3.D Risk Factors) and P3 (Item 5 Competition, citing AFAC)
competitive_position.claim: Volaris faces increasing industry capacity competition in Mexico, where commercial aircraft in service rose 11% from 389 in 2024 to 433 in 2025, Aeroenlaces Nacionales grew to 101 aircraft, Grupo Aeroméxico operated 132 and 34 aircraft at Aeroméxico and Aeroméxico Connect, and state-owned New Mexicana de Aviación launched in 2023.
quotes: As of December 31, 2025, the number of commercial aircraft in service in Mexico increased to 433, as compared to 389 as of December 31, 2024, according to AFAC.
Aeroenlaces Nacionales, our largest competitor by domestic market share in 2025, increased its fleet from 96 as of December 31, 2024 to 101 as of December 31, 2025, according to AFAC.
The New Mexicana de Aviación was created on June 15, 2023, as a state-owned company and started operations on December 26, 2023, further increasing our competition.

competitive_position.claim: Industry susceptibility to price discounting on unsold seats, competitors unbundling services, and rivals with greater financial resources and cheaper capital threaten Volaris' fares and cost advantage.
quotes: The airline industry is particularly susceptible to price discounting, because once a flight is scheduled, airlines incur only nominal additional costs to provide service to passengers occupying otherwise unsold seats.
Moreover, other airlines have begun to unbundle services by charging separate fees for services such as baggage transported, food and beverages consumed onboard and advance seat selection.

Any such competitor may have greater financial resources and access to cheaper sources of capital than we do, which could enable them to operate their business with a lower cost structure than we can.

competitive_position.basis: stated in P2 (Item 3.D Risk Factors) and P3 (Item 5 Competition, citing SICT)
competitive_position.claim: On domestic routes, Volaris faces substitution competition from Mexico's bus industry—which recorded approximately 3.1 billion passenger segments in 2024—as well as automobiles and video teleconferencing.
quotes: On our domestic routes, we face competition from other transportation alternatives, such as bus or automobile.

There is a large bus industry in Mexico, with total passenger segments of approximately 3.1 billion in 2024, of which approximately 84.6 million were executive and luxury passenger segments, according to the SICT in Mexico and which could include both long- and short-distance travel.

competitive_position.claim: AFAC slot reductions at Mexico City International Airport, cut from 61 to 52 and then to 43 flights per hour before a 2025 increase to 44, forced Volaris to reduce capacity there and redeploy six aircraft by end-2024.
quotes: Subsequently, on August 31, 2023, AFAC issued a resolution that further reduced the number of flights in the Mexico City International Airport to a maximum of 43 flights per hour.

In response to this reduction, which took effect on January 8, 2024, we reduced capacity at the Mexico City International Airport, initially redeploying four aircraft lines to other domestic airports, with a total of six aircraft redeployed by the end of 2024.
In May 2025, the AFAC authorized a limited increase in the maximum number of operations at the Mexico City International Airport from 43 to 44 flights per hour.

competitive_position.basis: stated in P2 (Item 3.D Risk Factors) and P4 (Q3 2026 6-K derivative annex and guidance table)
competitive_position.claim: Fuel represented 31% of Volaris' total operating costs in 2025, leaving results exposed to the 2026 Middle East conflict fuel spike without jet fuel derivatives in its 2026 third-quarter report, with fourth-quarter 2026 guidance assuming ~$4.40 per gallon versus $2.13 a year earlier.
quotes: The cost of fuel accounted for 38%, 33%, and 31%, of our total operating costs in 2023, 2024, and 2025, respectively.
The recent spike in the price of aircraft fuel resulting from the conflicts in Iran and the Middle East is expected to have an immediate and substantial negative impact on our results of operations.
As of the date of this report, Volaris does not have Jet Fuel derivative financial instruments.

competitive_position.basis: stated in P2 (Item 3.D Risk Factors) and P4 (Q3 2026 6-K derivative annex)
competitive_position.claim: Volaris faces demand and currency risks from slowing Mexican GDP growth (0.8% in 2025) and U.S. immigration and tariff policy uncertainty affecting U.S.–Mexico transborder travel, across 59% domestic and 41% international 2025 revenues with no foreign exchange derivatives in its 2026 third-quarter report.
quotes: For the year ended December 31, 2025, 59% of our total revenues were attributable to our Mexican domestic operations.
In 2023, 2024, and 2025, the Mexican economy grew 3.2%, 1.2% and 0.8%, respectively, in terms of gross domestic product (“GDP”), according to the INEGI.

This uncertainty is driven by changes in the U.S. presidential administration with respect to immigration policies, trade policies, treaties, tariffs, taxes, and other limitations on cross-border operations, which has impacted the demand for U.S.—Mexican transborder travel.
As of the date of presentation of this report, Volaris does not have foreign exchange derivative financial instruments.

competitive_position.basis: stated in P3 (Item 5 Operating Expenses) and P4 (Q3 2026 6-K outlook disclosures)

competitive_position.basis: stated in P1 (Item 4 Concession and Permits) and P2 (Item 3.D Risk Factors)
competitive_position.claim: Volaris faces legal and operational threats from potential SICT fare regulation if effective competition is deemed lacking, uncompensated concession revocation, violent crime in Mexico, and airspace closures or restrictions.
quotes: The imposition of fare regulations by the SICT could materially affect our business, results of operations and financial condition.
In the event that our Concession is revoked for any of the reasons specified above, we will not be entitled to any compensation, and we will be unable to continue to conduct our business.
Closures or restrictions of airspace can affect Volaris’s operations.
